works.picture: A low stone vault of Roman brick lit by one lamp, wine casks on their sides in two rows, a cooper driving a hoop.
works.source: invented in the period's manner; the flag unlock_plot_rotomagus (set by the chains wine_fleet and rollo_911; it has no row yet in story/unlocks_793.json) and the card harbour.chain_wine_fleet.end_own (a shared cellar under the south wall). Roman vaults reused under the wall are a guess (?)

works.name: A stair and a ring at the river gate
works.what: Oak piles and a laid bed of brushwood and stone on the mud beside the gate, with a ring post and a plank stair, so a boat can lie upright and load dry at any state of the tide.
works.needs: The tollman's leave, since the strand is the king's (after 911 the count's); a neap tide for the work.
works.gives: Loading here takes half the time and porters cost less; the boat does not strain on the mud at the ebb; a skiff can be kept on the ring.
works.picture: Men driving oak piles into grey mud at low water under a wall of mixed Roman stone, a small boat lying on her side nearby.
works.source: invented; no dug quay of this age is known at Rouen and boats lay on the strand (dossier 1). Timber-and-brushwood hards as at Dorestad (?)

works.name: A table at Saint Peter's gate
works.what: A cauldron, a table and a year's rye for the abbey's gate, where the poor are fed in the hungry years; the brothers do the cooking and say whose gift it is.
works.needs: Rye or wheat in the hold, or silver to buy it at the king's price and no higher.
works.gives: flag hy_fed_poor and deed gave_alms; the abbey remembers the house: lodging and a leech for a sick crewman without asking, and the brothers' word with other abbeys on the Seine.
works.picture: A line of thin people with wooden bowls at an abbey gate, a monk ladling pottage from a black cauldron, bare trees behind.
works.source: the famine of 792-794 and the king's order that bishops, abbots and counts feed the poor (spine thread hungry_years; Frankfurt 794 c. 4 for the price of grain). That Saint Peter's fed two hundred is invented

works.name: A share in the cathedral's ransom chest
works.what: Silver given to the chest the clerk Einold keeps, out of which the city's taken people are bought back from the fleets, one at a time, as word of them comes.
works.needs: To have carried a name for Einold at least once, so he knows the silver is not a Northman's joke.
works.gives: deed gave_alms, and bought_captives counted for you and not against; each year one of the ransomed comes to your boat to work a season without pay; Einold tells you where the fleets lie.
works.picture: An iron-bound chest open on a church floor, a grey clerk weighing cut silver on a small balance, a list of names pinned under a stone.
works.source: invented; buying back captives as a good work (Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 15 and 35, Robinson 1921); the captives of 841 (Annales Bertiniani). The chronicle of Fontenelle's 68 captives bought for 26 pounds is unchecked (?)

works.name: A pillar in the archbishop's crypt
works.what: The cost of one carved pillar and its vault in the crypt Archbishop Robert is building under the new choir of Saint Mary's. The mason cuts a small ship on the capital, low down, where a kneeling man would see it.
works.needs: An audience with the archbishop, and stone: he will take part of the price in English lead or in glass.
works.gives: The house has a place in the cathedral: a Mass on the day you name, burial for your dead in the city, the archbishop's commissions, and a mark that will still be there when the game ends.
works.picture: A low round-arched crypt with short thick pillars, lit by candles; a mason on his knees cutting a small ship into a capital.
works.source: the choir over a crypt begun about 1030 by Archbishop Robert, finished by Maurilius and dedicated 1 October 1063; the crypt survives (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathédrale_Notre-Dame_de_Rouen). The ship on the capital is invented

ships.how: built to order over a winter, or hired with her men by the trip
ships.note: Above the city the tide is no help and the wine comes down in flat barges, towed up empty and poled down full. The wrights of the east stream build them from the oak of the forest behind the city.
ships.picture: A long flat barge with square ends, deep in brown water under two rows of casks, a man at a long steering oar and the city wall behind.
ships.source: sea ships to the wall on the flood, barges above (traffic_793.json; dossier 4); Design/content/ships.md. The yard is invented

ships.how: lent by the archbishop or an abbot to a shipman who has kept his commissions (story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_river_estate_ship)
ships.note: The abbeys of the Seine send their own wine down and their salt up in their own ships, toll-free where their charters run. A lord's ship is not sold; she is entrusted.
ships.picture: A broad river ship with a carved stem and a cross on a pole at the bow, monks' servants loading casks, lead roofs in the valley behind.
ships.source: story/ships_793.json (built at rotomagus); the toll freedom of Saint-Germain's boats here, 779 (Tardif no. 81)

ships.how: bought second-hand from a fisherman under the wall
ships.note: The salmon and the small spring fish are netted from open plank boats that work the tide off the strand. One comes up for sale when a man grows too old for the wave.
ships.picture: A small open plank boat with two oars and a wet net, a basket of silver fish on the thwart, grounded on mud under a wall.
ships.source: salmon and the small fish at Rouen: Ibrahim ibn Ya'qub (960s), retold; Design/content/ships.md

ships.how: bought for 40 d, or built in a fortnight
ships.note: For crossing to the south bank, for lightering casks out to a ship that cannot wait for the tide, and for going quietly down to Saint-Wandrille.
ships.picture: A short flat skiff with one man standing to pole, a single cask amidships, a ship aground beyond.
ships.source: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_skiff_punt (40 d, this port named)

ships.how: hired by the crossing; not for sale
ships.note: There is no bridge. Carts, cattle and, in the year 800, a king cross the Seine here by boat.
ships.picture: A wide flat ferry with an ox cart and two horses aboard, four men at sweeps, the far bank low and green.
ships.source: the king crossed the Seine at Rouen in 800, how is not said (Annales regni Francorum); the ferry is the project's (traffic_793.json). The stone bridge is twelfth-century

ships.how: bought second-hand on the strand, seldom; after 841 more often, from men leaving the trade
ships.note: The merchants of the city have sea ships: twenty-eight of them came up on one tide in the spring of 841. They are built on other shores and change hands here.
ships.picture: A deep round-bellied sailing ship with one square sail furled, aground and leaning under the south wall, her owner arguing price with two men.
ships.source: Nithard II.6 (merchant ships at Rouen, 841); story/ships_793.json does not build the class here, so second-hand only

ships.how: bought second-hand from a settler who has turned farmer
ships.note: A man given land by the rope has a ship he no longer needs. The Northmen's wrights on the east stream keep such hulls afloat for a generation, and lay down no new ones of this kind.
ships.picture: A long low clinker ship with a high curved stem on blocks by a red-running stream, a wright with an adze, a ploughed field behind.
ships.source: the grant of 911 and the land shared out by the rope (Dudo ii, LATER); ships found on the river at Rouen in 885 (Annales Vedastini). story/ships_793.json builds this class new only in the north and only to 900: here it is second-hand, kept afloat by Norse wrights settled on the Seine, and gone by about 940 (?)

sayings.text: A seething tide carried the ships up from the river mouth and set them down by the city.
sayings.source: Nithard, Histories II.6, on the spring of 841, in the dossier's own rendering of the Latin, shortened

sayings.text: They raged with plunder, sword and fire, and gave the city, the monks and the rest of the people to killing and captivity.
The king takes a tenth. The river takes what it likes.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (the tollman's)

sayings.text: What use are these little rags? In bed they do not cover me, on a horse they keep off neither wind nor rain. So the king said of the short Frisian cloaks, and he was paying the old price.
sayings.source: Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34, retold in our own words (Grant 1907 not quoted). Said at Adalsind's whenever a Frisian comes in

sayings.text: A Northman was told to kiss the king's foot for his land. He lifted the foot to his mouth instead of bending, and the king went over on his back.
sayings.source: Dudo of Saint-Quentin ii (about 1015, LATER), retold; told on the strand after 911, of one of Rollo's men and not of Rollo

sayings.text: Six winters ago he had no beard. Now it is past his knees. In this city even the hair is in a hurry to get to the river.
sayings.source: the young man of Rouen seen by Ibrahim ibn Ya'qub in the 960s, retold; the joke is invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: Bound, I bind. Iron made me and I hold what is stronger than I am.
sayings.source: a plain rendering of the sense of Symphosius, riddle 5, Catena (Riese 1894); the Latin is in texts_793.json symphosius_05_catena. On this strand after 841 nobody laughs at the answer

sayings.text: Rollo hung gold on an oak for three years. Our priest cannot leave a candle on the altar overnight.
sayings.source: the arm rings at 'Rollo's Mere': William of Jumieges ii (LATER), retold; the complaint is invented

sayings.text: No one is to give or sell a mail coat, arms or a horse to the Northmen, for any reason or any ransom, on pain of his life.
sayings.source: Edictum Pistense c. 25, 864 (MGH Capit. II no. 273), our rendering, shortened

sayings.text: The ink is thin, the leaf is rough, and the wind comes off the river under the door. Thank God it grows dark.
sayings.source: invented in the manner of the scribes' marginal complaints of the ninth century (Hildhard's boys)

sayings.text: A full cask keeps. A full man does not.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (the cooper's)

easter_eggs.text: The small silver fish sold on wet leaves in the market smells of cucumber when it is fresh. A traveller from Spain noticed the same thing a hundred and seventy years later and wrote it down.
easter_eggs.source: Ibrahim ibn Ya'qub (960s), retold; the fish is the smelt, which does smell so

easter_eggs.text: In a hard winter a white goose with a red beak and red feet comes to the river. The people call it something like 'gansh'.
easter_eggs.source: Ibrahim ibn Ya'qub (960s), retold from the French given at fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouen

easter_eggs.text: A block built into the south wall upside down has letters on it and half a carved wreath. The wall was put up in a hurry six lifetimes ago out of whatever was standing.
easter_eggs.source: the wall of about 325-350 built from torn-down buildings (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortifications_de_Rouen); the block is invented

easter_eggs.text: The old say that Bishop Romanus tore the dedication off a temple of Venus in the round house and the temple fell, and that he turned back a flood with his staff. Nobody here has heard of a dragon. That story will not be told for six hundred years.
easter_eggs.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanus_of_Rouen; the dragon first written in 1394 (dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: After 911 the stream by the slip has a new name. The Northmen call it the red brook, for the dyers' water, and the name sticks: Rodobech in a charter of about 1020. The single wave that runs up the river on the big tides gets a Norse name too.
easter_eggs.source: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robec; fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascaret (la barre, from Norse bara, wave)

easter_eggs.text: From about 1010 the town tells of the count's brother, kept five years in the tower, who went out of the high window one night on a very long rope and was not seen again in the city.
easter_eggs.source: William of Jumieges v (LATER): Count William, brother of Richard II

easter_eggs.text: A lid has slid off one of the stone coffins on the slope. Inside there is a little glass bottle, whole, and nothing else that can be named.
easter_eggs.source: the Roman and early Christian grave field with stone coffins at Saint-Gervais (fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Église_Saint-Gervais_de_Rouen); the bottle is invented in keeping with such graves

easter_eggs.text: In the 970s a moneyer's tray holds, among thousands of the count's and the archbishop's pennies, two of a boy king of the English who reigned three years. Somebody will bury them all in two pots near Fecamp and not come back.
easter_eggs.source: the Fecamp hoard, buried about 980-985: 3,107 Rouen pennies of Richard I, 2,478 read as Archbishop Hugh's, two of Edward the Martyr (hoards_793.json fecamp; F. Dumas, CRAI 1971)

easter_eggs.text: In 820 a dark, silent lord from the Spanish march lodges in the city with two servants. He lost a duel on horseback before the emperor and his life was spared. He walks on the wall every evening and looks south.
easter_eggs.source: Bera, count of Barcelona, exiled to Rouen: Annales regni Francorum 820

easter_eggs.text: The roofs at Saint-Wandrille are grey and dull because they are lead, and the lead is English. The abbot who put it there took the king's tolls for twenty years and was King Offa's dearest friend, in the king's own words.
easter_eggs.source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12; that the lead was English is likely and not stated (?)
